articles.title: Wild new Aston Martin Valen is a V12 brute with 838bhp
articles.title_tr: Wild new Aston Martin Valen is a V12 brute with 838bhp
articles.summary:
Vanquish-based hyper-GT is priced from £1.5m and offers almost unlimited personalisation

Aston Martin has transformed the Vanquish into a V12-engined hyper-GT called the Valen that has more power than any other front-engined road car on sale.
The radical new Valen is the latest ultra-exclusive model from Aston Martin's Special Vehicles Operations division, which created the Vulcan track car, DBR22 speedster and the one-off Victor hypercar.
The new hyper-GT packs the 5.2-litre twin-turbo V12 from the Vanquish but ramps the power output to 838bhp, making it more powerful than any Aston apart from the mid-engined Valhalla and Valkyrie.
Torque stands at 738lb ft and the Valen can dispatch 0-62mph in 3.1sec, the same time as the Porsche 911 GT3 RS.
The Valen's Vanquish origins are clear from its silhouette but it has been extensively overhauled inside and out in line with its heightened performance and exclusivity. High levels of personalisation will mean no two of the 150 customer cars will look the same.

Although the Valen's striking appearance nods to the original DBS and its successor, the Vantage, Aston Martin creative chief Marek Reichman said it is a significant departure from past models.
"Valen gave us the opportunity to explore and express more extreme emotions through a new form language and surface treatment," he said.
Defining features include the brutish new snout—which takes the signature Aston Martin grille motif and expands it across the entire front end—as well as the chunky ducktail spoiler, the aggressive slimline LED lights and, most obviously, the GT3-style carbonfibre aerodynamic addenda, including a huge rear diffuser and downforce-boosting side skirts.

There's an eye-catching new exhaust set-up too, with two exits in the diffuser and two through its centre. The uppermost exits are always open, while the lower set is valved, opening in the raciest drive modes.
The use of carbonfibre, aluminium, titanium and magnesium has helped to make the Valen as much as 110kg lighter than its Vanquish counterpart. The optional lightweight pack alone saves 16.9kg, bringing machined-aluminium suspension arms and knuckles, plus titanium chassis bolts.
Meanwhile, the gearbox has been remapped with the software from Aston Martin's Vantage GT4 race car, giving more aggressive shifts. The throttle pedal's behaviour has also been modified so it is more sensitive in the road-focused Sport and Sport+ drive modes, while the throttle's travel is extended in Track mode for "when on-limit precision is the priority".

The suspension has also been stiffened by way of new springs and the steering response has been quickened for improved responsiveness—completing the Vanquish's transition from super-GT to no-holds-barred performance weapon.
Simon Newton, Aston Martin's director of vehicle performance, suggested the ambition was to unleash the latent sporting potential of the Vanquish.
"Valen channels the more overt dynamic purpose of a true sports car," said Newton, who added that the revisions "intensify the character of Aston Martin's signature GT."
Each of the 150 examples of the Valen will be priced at £1.5 million—before buyers delve into an extensive catalogue of optional extras. These include an exposed-carbonfibre exterior finish that can be tinted to whichever colour the customer wishes, through Aston Martin's Q division. The Valen also makes extensive use of 3D printing, such as around the centre console.

articles.title: Watch God Of War Laufey Star Smash The Last Of Us Golf Club Prop On Her First Day
articles.title_tr: Watch God Of War Laufey Star Smash The Last Of Us Golf Club Prop On Her First Day
articles.summary:
Deborah Ann Woll plays Faye in the upcoming PS5 game God of War Laufey, and she had quite a memorable first day on set. At San Diego Comic-Con recently, she shared a story about how, on her very first day, she broke a famous prop from The Last of Us due to her strength and tenacity--only she didn't know the significance at the time. And now, footage of the event has arrived.



"Unbeknownst to me, this was a very famous prop that they had used on The Last of Us," she said, going on to joke that it was "some sort of sporting equipment." It was actually a golf club prop, and you probably know what that means...



"They gave it to me and I was supposed to use it like an axe. And I broke it," Woll said.



Game director Ariel Lawrence added, "She swung it so hard, it cracked. And it echoed throughout the volume. And we were like, 'Hot damn, let's go.'"




https://twitter.com/SonySantaMonica/status/2088280064974635337




God of War: Laufey is in the works now for PS5, and it's arriving in February 2027. Starring alongside Woll is The Boys actor Jack Quaid, who plays a gelatinous cube named Phranque. 



A new Kratos-led game is coming after that, and it will pick up where Laufey left off.

articles.title: McLaren's manual revival shows the art of stick-shifting isn't dead
articles.title_tr: McLaren's manual revival shows the art of stick-shifting isn't dead
articles.summary:
Row-your-own sports cars are endangered, but they give so much more engagement than an auto

There is no longer any objective argument to be made for the manual gearbox or, by extension, against the automatic gearbox. Automatics, whether dual-clutch or of the conventional planetary type, are faster, smoother, more convenient and more efficient than the old-fashioned H-pattern transmission with a lever and a clutch pedal.
This, then, is not an objective argument but an emotional one. I love a good manual gearbox, and I'm extremely pleased cars like the new McLaren McL 6GT are bringing them back in a big way. 
Once upon a time, automatic gearboxes were slow and wasted energy with their slushy torque converters, while automated manuals were slow and jerky. Some are still a bit like that, but many now operate with clinical efficiency.
Even so, at best automatics bore me. They go about their business smoothly and quickly but, even if they have a responsive manual mode and some tactile paddles, as a driver I don’t feel like an essential part of the equation.
As a result, any driving satisfaction is necessarily derived from winding the engine out and pushing the chassis. Everything else is just transit. But those delights require a certain level of commitment and speed, which isn’t always possible, let alone advisable, on the road.
Add a good manual gearbox into the mix and everything changes. ‘Good’ is an important caveat, it must be said. What constitutes ‘good’ varies by personal taste, but it’s uncontroversial to say that long-throw, baggy shifts are no good to anyone. If the action is precise and mechanical, however, with a predictable and manageable throw on the clutch pedal, a manual adds a huge extra dimension to driving.
Straights, boring A-roads and jaunts through town become an opportunity to interact with the mechanicals of the car, to hone your skill. Every manual car has a certain speed and cadence of gearchange where the lever slips effortlessly out of one gear and then almost gets sucked into the next. Finding it can take a bit of time and attention, but it’s very satisfying when you do.
It’s the same with rev-matching on downshifts. Of course, you can just slip the clutch a bit and lurch into a lower gear. The driving test doesn’t require anything more sophisticated and it works fine for most people. But once you master the art of heel-and-toeing to match engine speed and gearbox speed for seamless downchanges, it’s a game you can play over and over again, no matter whether you’re on a track day or going between third and second in traffic.
I can see how that’s perceived as a chore if you’re just trying to get from A to B, but I’m never just going from A to B: I’d like to enjoy the driving while I’m at it, even if it’s not a special journey. I don’t care that the auto is faster: you can’t go very fast on the road anyway and I’m not in a race. I want to savour the mechanical interaction.
McLaren gets this. In creating the new six-speed McL 6GT, it says it has strived to achieve the strongest link between man and machine possible, to give "a form of driving connection that is increasingly rare: tactile, analogue, and deeply mechanical".
"Every shift, throttle movement and steering input is intended to feel deliberate, physical, and rewarding, connecting the driver to the machine," it says. "This mechanical character extends beyond the drivetrain. Hydraulic steering, tactile switchgear, and visible engineering details all contribute to a sense of purity of involvement for the driver." Promising. 
 
With hybrids, electric cars and combustion engine bans, things are only heading one way for the manual, and I find the idea of simulated gearboxes – like that in the new Ferrari 12Cilindri Manuale – a bit too ‘vegan sausage’ to be more than a whimsical gimmick.
Perhaps surprisingly, then, the EV transition doesn’t bother me too much, because I find having no gearbox preferable to an automatic one, since it can afford instant responses and I like the mechanical purity of an EV.
As a result, a two-car garage of an EV and something old with a really special engine and a manual gearbox would probably keep me happy.
What would it be, though? The Frontline MGB restomod that I drove last year, with its Mazda MX-5-sourced six-speed, had my favourite manual shift so far – not a bad place to start.

Once upon a time, automatic gearboxes were slow and wasted energy with their slushy torque converters, while automated manuals were slow and jerky. Some are still a bit like that, but many now operate with clinical efficiency.
Even so, at best automatics bore me. They go about their business smoothly and quickly but, even if they have a responsive manual mode and some tactile paddles, as a driver I don’t feel like an essential part of the equation.
As a result, any driving satisfaction is necessarily derived from winding the engine out and pushing the chassis. Everything else is just transit. But those delights require a certain level of commitment and speed, which isn’t always possible, let alone advisable, on the road.
Add a good manual gearbox into the mix and everything changes. ‘Good’ is an important caveat, it must be said. What constitutes ‘good’ varies by personal taste, but it’s uncontroversial to say that long-throw, baggy shifts are no good to anyone. If the action is precise and mechanical, however, with a predictable and manageable throw on the clutch pedal, a manual adds a huge extra dimension to driving.
Straights, boring A-roads and jaunts through town become an opportunity to interact with the mechanicals of the car, to hone your skill. Every manual car has a certain speed and cadence of gearchange where the lever slips effortlessly out of one gear and then almost gets sucked into the next. Finding it can take a bit of time and attention, but it’s very satisfying when you do.
It’s the same with rev-matching on downshifts. Of course, you can just slip the clutch a bit and lurch into a lower gear. The driving test doesn’t require anything more sophisticated and it works fine for most people. But once you master the art of heel-and-toeing to match engine speed and gearbox speed for seamless downchanges, it’s a game you can play over and over again, no matter whether you’re on a track day or going between third and second in traffic.
I can see how that’s perceived as a chore if you’re just trying to get from A to B, but I’m never just going from A to B: I’d like to enjoy the driving while I’m at it, even if it’s not a special journey. I don’t care that the auto is faster: you can’t go very fast on the road anyway and I’m not in a race. I want to savour the mechanical interaction.
McLaren gets this. In creating the new six-speed McL 6GT, it says it has strived to achieve the strongest link between man and machine possible, to give "a form of driving connection that is increasingly rare: tactile, analogue, and deeply mechanical".
"Every shift, throttle movement and steering input is intended to feel deliberate, physical, and rewarding, connecting the driver to the machine," it says. "This mechanical character extends beyond the drivetrain. Hydraulic steering, tactile switchgear, and visible engineering details all contribute to a sense of purity of involvement for the driver." Promising. 
 
With hybrids, electric cars and combustion engine bans, things are only heading one way for the manual, and I find the idea of simulated gearboxes – like that in the new Ferrari 12Cilindri Manuale – a bit too ‘vegan sausage’ to be more than a whimsical gimmick.
Perhaps surprisingly, then, the EV transition doesn’t bother me too much, because I find having no gearbox preferable to an automatic one, since it can afford instant responses and I like the mechanical purity of an EV.
As a result, a two-car garage of an EV and something old with a really special engine and a manual gearbox would probably keep me happy.
What would it be, though? The Frontline MGB restomod that I drove last year, with its Mazda MX-5-sourced six-speed, had my favourite manual shift so far – not a bad place to start.
